beats.say: Welcome to the last module.
Bring it together: every question here maps back to an earlier module.

scenes.title: Flashcards: answer, then flip
rows: Which kind of model learns p(x, y)?
Which kind learns p(y | x) directly?

beats.say: Start with the flashcards. Each card asks one key idea. Try to answer before you flip it.
Card one: which kind of model learns the joint probability of x and y?
Flip it: generative.
Card two: which kind learns the label given the data, directly? Discriminative.
Cards three to five: naive Bayes is generative; logistic regression and an S V M are discriminative.
Recalling an idea, rather than rereading it, is what makes it stick.

scenes.title: The ideas that come up again and again

beats.say: These are the core ideas to revise.
Gradient descent.
The bias variance trade-off.
Regularisation.
Evaluation metrics.
And generative versus discriminative models.
One pair worth getting straight.
Generative models learn the joint probability of x and y.
In other words, how the data is produced.
Naive Bayes is one.
Discriminative models learn the probability of the label given the data, directly.
Logistic regression and an S V M are discriminative.
Finally, a research spotlight.
Video evidence goes into a multimodal large language model.
The prompt shapes how the model reasons about it.
Out comes a forensic video analysis: the whole course applied to a real research question.

scenes.title: Generative vs discriminative: which models p(x, y), how the data is produced?
scenes.good: That's right. Generative models learn the joint distribution p of x and y, like naive Bayes. Discriminative models learn p of y given x directly, like logistic regression or an S V M.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Generative models learn the joint distribution p of x and y, like naive Bayes. Discriminative models learn p of y given x directly, like logistic regression or an S V M.

beats.say: Quick check.
